The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was an effort to ensure voting rights for African Americans and other racial minorities by prohibiting racial discrimination in voting. [d1] The Act explicitly states that "no voting qualification or prerequisite to voting, or standard, practice, or procedure shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color." [d5] The law aimed to overcome legal barriers at the state and local levels that prevented African Americans from exercising their right to vote as guaranteed under the 15th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. [d4] Congress adopted the law to ensure that states followed the 15th Amendment's guarantee that the right to vote not be denied because of race, fundamentally opening political opportunities for Black and brown communities. [d7] The Act provided for direct federal intervention to enable African Americans to register and vote and banned tactics long designed to keep them from the polls, such as literacy tests and poll taxes. [d9] More broadly, the Act codifies the 15th Amendment's permanent guarantee that no person shall be denied the right to vote on account of race or color, adopted at a time when African Americans were substantially disenfranchised in many Southern states.
